<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par142 />{{GHGmargin-letter|142|d}}
Rem. 1. The close relation between verbal-clauses beginning with the subject and actual noun-clauses, is seen finally from the fact that the former also are somewhat frequently added with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (or subordinated) to a preceding sentence in order to lay stress upon some accompanying circumstance; on such noun-clauses describing a ''state'' or ''circumstance'', cf. {{GHGpar|141|e}}. This is especially the case, again, when the circumstantial appendage involves an antithesis; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=18}} ''seeing that'' nevertheless ''Abraham shall surely become'', &c.; 24:56, 26:27, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=22}}, and such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=2.4}}, 29:17, where by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} a new subject is introduced in express antithesis to one just mentioned. Moreover, in the examples treated above, under ''b'' and ''c'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}}, &c.), the subject is frequently introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, which then corresponds to the Greek δέ, used to interpose an explanation, &c., see Winer, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des neutest. Sprachidioms}}, § 53. 7 ''b''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|e}}
2. By a peculiar construction verbal-clauses may be joined by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} and a following subject to participial clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=הִיא מוּצֵאת וְהִיא שָֽׁלְחָה|translate=she was already brought forth, when she sent}}, &c.; 44:3, 4, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=8}}; for other examples, see {{GHGpar|116|u}} (where it is pointed out, note 1, that the apodosis also frequently appears in the form of a ''noun''-clause, a further proof of the close relation between verbal-clauses beginning with the subject and noun-clauses proper). Without doubt there is in all these cases a kind of inversion of the principal clause and the temporal subordinate clause; the latter for the sake of greater emphasis being raised to an independent noun-clause, while the real principal action is added as though it were an accompanying circumstance, and hence in the form of an ordinary circumstantial clause. [Cf. Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 166 ff.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|f}}
'''2.''' According to what has been remarked above, under ''a'', the natural ''order of words'' within the verbal sentence is: ''Verb—Subject'', or ''Verb—Subject—Object''. But as in the noun-clause ({{GHGpar|141|l}}) so also in the verbal-clause, a variation of the usual order of words frequently occurs when any member of the sentence is to be specially emphasized by priority of position.<ref>Not infrequently also the striving after ''chiasmus'' mentioned in {{GHGpar|114|r}}, note, occasions a departure from the usual arrangement of words.</ref> Thus the order may be:—

(''a'') ''Object—Verb—Subject'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=19}} and frequently. Naturally the examples are far more numerous, in which the object precedes a verbal form which includes the subject in itself, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=10.14.18}}, 6:16, 8:17, 9:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=22|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=5}}, &c.

(''b'') ''Verb—Object—Subject'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=16}} (but {{GHGheb|text=המלאך}} is probably only a subsequent addition); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=19}}, &c.

(''c'') ''Subject—Object—Verb'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=12|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=25}}.<ref>This sequence occurs even in prose ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, &c.); it is, however, more doubtful here than in the above prophetical and poetical passages, whether the preceding subject should not be regarded rather as the subject of a compound sentence (§ 143), the predicate of which is an independent verbal-clause; this would explain why the verbal-clause is usually separated from the subject by one of the greater disjunctives.—On the other hand, the sequence ''Subject''—''Object''—{{GHGterm|Verb}} is quite common in Aramaic (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=2|verse=7}}, 10); cf. Gesenius, ''Comm.'' on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=24}}, and Kautzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, § 84. 1 ''b''. The pure Aramaic usage of placing the ''object'' before the {{GHGterm|infinitive}} occurs in Hebrew in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=21|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=28|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=36|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (?).</ref><section end=par142 /><noinclude>
